title: Track where inquiries originate
check: Can you identify the source of recent inquiries without guessing?
evidence: Review your last 10 inquiries (or all if fewer). Each should have a source such as referral, search, email or a named campaign. Use counts only; do not copy customer details here.
action: Add one source field to your lead record. Use campaign-specific links where appropriate, or ask a short ‘How did you find us?’ question. Record unknown explicitly rather than inventing attribution.
verify: Send a synthetic inquiry from one tagged link and confirm its source survives into your lead record.

title: Match the promise to the destination
check: Does each active promotion lead to a page that delivers the same offer and next step?
evidence: Open your most-used promotion, then its destination. Compare the promised deliverable, audience, price and call to action.
action: Choose one promotion. Make its headline and destination describe the same concrete outcome. Remove obsolete prices and claims you cannot support.
verify: Ask someone to read the promotion and destination and describe what they expect to receive; compare that description to your actual delivery.

title: Test the real mobile path
check: Can a mobile visitor reach and use your primary next step without a broken link or obstructing layout?
evidence: Use an actual phone to follow the public link. Check the headline, buttons, form labels and navigation; note any failed step.
action: Fix the first broken or hidden primary action. Shorten oversized sections, make controls readable, and remove overlays that block the form or checkout.
verify: Repeat the same path on the phone from a fresh tab and complete a safe test submission.

title: Separate qualified interest from visits
check: Do you know which traffic source produces inquiries that fit what you can deliver?
evidence: For one consistent recent period, compare visits, inquiries and qualified inquiries per source when those counts are available. Record missing counts as unknown.
action: Write a simple fit rule: service needed, location if relevant, timing and delivery capacity. Tally sources against that rule before increasing promotion or spending.
verify: Apply the same rule to the next five inquiries and record the result. Small counts are directional evidence, not proof of a reliable conversion rate.

title: Name the buyer and deliverable
check: Can a visitor tell who the offer is for and exactly what they receive?
evidence: Read only the top of the offer page. Look for a specific buyer, problem, deliverable and next step.
action: Use: ‘For [buyer] who needs [problem solved], receive [specific deliverable] so you can [practical use].’ Replace vague ‘AI-powered growth’ language with what the buyer can actually use.
verify: Give the sentence to someone unfamiliar with the offer and ask them to name the deliverable without extra explanation.

title: Make scope and total cost clear
check: Are inclusions, exclusions, total price and any recurring charges visible before a buyer commits?
evidence: Compare the offer page, order summary and actual delivery scope. Look for ambiguous support, setup or subscription costs.
action: List what is included, what is excluded, the one-time or recurring price, and required third-party tools. Keep prices consistent with checkout; obtain owner approval for pricing changes.
verify: Walk through the purchase path and confirm no material charge or required tool first appears after payment.

title: Show evidence you can stand behind
check: Does the page show an accurate sample or demonstration without invented testimonials or unsupported results?
evidence: Open the sample yourself. Check that it represents the current deliverable; confirm you have permission to use any customer example.
fix: Replace claims with a real sample
action: Create a small representative excerpt or clearly labeled synthetic demonstration. State what it shows and its limits. Remove revenue or performance claims you cannot substantiate.
verify: Compare the sample to what a buyer receives today; each advertised function should exist and work.

title: State delivery and support boundaries
check: Does the buyer know the delivery method, expected timing and how to get help?
evidence: Locate delivery instructions and a monitored support route. Check that advertised timing matches a completed delivery test.
fix: Write a delivery promise you can keep
action: State the file or service format, delivery trigger, realistic timing, support contact and any limits. Do not promise instant access until it has been verified end to end.
verify: Follow the buyer instructions from a completed safe test and confirm the deliverable opens and support requests reach the intended inbox or queue.

title: Make the primary action unmistakable
check: Is there one clear primary next step with wording that explains what happens?
evidence: View the page without scrolling first, then at its end. Identify competing buttons or unclear labels such as ‘Go’ or ‘Submit’.
action: Use a specific label such as ‘Request a quote’ or ‘Get the checklist’. Align repeated primary buttons to the same destination and explain any required payment or contact details.
verify: Ask a new visitor what happens after clicking the button; confirm their answer matches the next screen.

title: Ask only for necessary information
check: Can a buyer or lead complete the form without unnecessary or sensitive fields?
evidence: For each required field, state why it is needed at this step. Confirm labels, field types and helpful error messages.
action: Keep only fields necessary to respond or fulfill the request. Move optional scoping questions later. Never request passwords, API keys or payment-card details in an ordinary intake form.
verify: Try an empty submission and an invalid email. Confirm errors are understandable and previously entered non-sensitive values are preserved.

title: Verify that submissions actually arrive
check: Has a recent test submission reached the system where someone will act on it?
evidence: Look for one labeled synthetic submission in the destination record, including its timestamp and expected non-sensitive fields.
action: Submit a clearly labeled test, then inspect the real receiving system. Fix the endpoint, field mapping or notification route if the record is missing. A success animation alone is not evidence.
verify: Confirm the stored record matches the submitted fields and that the designated owner can find it.

title: Explain submission and recovery
check: Does a visitor see an accurate confirmation, a next step and a fallback when submission fails?
evidence: Review both a successful submission and a safely simulated failure. Check consent wording and where the information goes.
fix: Add honest success and failure states
action: Show success only after the server accepts the record. Explain response expectations, data use and a contact alternative. On failure, preserve input and offer retry without claiming delivery.
verify: Test the success path and a controlled failure in a test environment. Confirm the two messages accurately describe their outcomes.

title: Give every inquiry an owner
check: Does each open inquiry have a responsible person and a next-action time?
evidence: Review a handful of open inquiries. Look for named ownership, current status and the next action; avoid copying personal information into this checklist.
action: Use a simple tracker with owner, stage, next action and due date. Assign new inquiries to a monitored queue before adding more automation.
verify: Create one test inquiry and confirm a real owner can identify what to do next and when.

title: Keep response promises realistic
check: Are incoming messages checked often enough to meet the response expectation you advertise?
evidence: Compare actual receipt and first-response times for recent inquiries with your public response wording.
fix: Set a response window you can meet
action: Choose coverage hours and a review routine that match capacity. Adjust unrealistic public promises with owner approval. Use an acknowledgment only if it accurately states when a person will respond.
verify: Measure the next few response intervals and confirm they meet the stated expectation; investigate any missed case.

title: Keep follow-up relevant and wanted
check: Does your follow-up relate to the request, honor opt-outs and avoid duplicate messages?
evidence: Review the actual message sequence and suppression controls. Distinguish replying to an inquiry from enrolling someone in marketing.
action: Draft a short response tied to the stated need, with one clear next step. Stop on opt-out or resolution. Get approval before activating outbound automation and check applicable messaging requirements.
verify: In a safe test, mark a test contact opted out and confirm no subsequent automated follow-up is queued for that contact.

title: Notice failures before leads go cold
check: Can you see failed deliveries, bounced messages and overdue follow-ups?
evidence: Inspect the actual error or overdue queue, not only the automation’s ‘enabled’ switch.
action: Collect failed sends and overdue next actions in one place a person reviews. Include a retry decision and owner. Avoid blindly retrying actions that could duplicate messages or charges.
verify: Safely simulate a failed action in a test environment and confirm it appears for review with a clear recovery step.

title: Confirm the order before payment
check: Does checkout show the correct deliverable, currency, amount and billing frequency?
evidence: Open checkout without paying. Compare the order summary to the offer and verify the merchant identity is correct.
action: Correct mismatched product text or links. Escalate price, currency or billing changes to the owner. Remove links to unavailable products from your active sales page.
verify: Repeat the buyer path and confirm all order details match before the payment button.

title: Test payment outcomes safely
check: Have success, decline and delayed-payment behavior been tested without fake transactions in live mode?
evidence: Find records from your payment provider’s sandbox or test mode. Check that an unpaid or declined order does not receive paid access.
action: Use the provider’s official sandbox or test environment to test success, failure and pending states. Verify server-side payment status rather than trusting a browser redirect or amount supplied by a visitor.
verify: Confirm paid test orders unlock the correct item while unpaid, failed and unrelated orders remain blocked.

title: Deliver the purchased item reliably
check: Can a paid buyer receive the right deliverable even if they close the checkout tab?
evidence: Trace a paid test order through the server-side fulfillment record and the actual buyer access or delivery route.
action: Use verified provider events and idempotent fulfillment so repeated events do not duplicate actions. Provide a receipt or recovery route that helps the buyer regain access without disclosing their purchase publicly.
verify: In test mode, replay the same completion event and simulate closing the success page. Confirm one correct fulfillment and a working recovery process.

title: Learn from completed and lost orders
check: Can you distinguish paid, pending, failed and refunded orders and record a useful reason for lost sales?
evidence: Review your order view and support process. Do not count a checkout visit, invoice or unpaid order as revenue.
fix: Track the outcome that actually happened
action: Record order status, collected amount and refunds from provider records. Note voluntary feedback on lost sales. Use comparable periods and acknowledge small samples before drawing conclusions.
verify: Reconcile a sample of order statuses with the provider dashboard and confirm your revenue total excludes unpaid orders and handles refunds consistently.
